records.text: earning. When education expanded broadly, productivity gains translated into shared prosperity. When skill formation lagged, inequality widened. Finally, diffusion has accelerated over time: each new innovation wave is more compressed than the last. The industrial revolution took half a century to spread. Railroads and steel diffused over several decades. Electrification and motorization required a generation of complementary investment. Electronics matured over roughly forty years. The internet reached mass adoption in less than thirty. Each successive wave has traveled faster than its predecessor, reflecting better communication, deeper capital markets, and accumulated institutional experience. If this pattern holds, artificial intelligence may diffuse faster still. Taken together, the historical record is clear. Innovation waves are disruptive, capital- intensive, and volatile. They displace workers, concentrate gains early, and provoke political backlash. But over time they raise productivity, restructure labor markets, expand output, and—when institutions adapt—improve living standards broadly. The speed of diffusion is increasing, compressing adjustment timelines. The lessons are not about whether transformation will occur, but about how society manages it.

The policy challenge mirrors earlier eras: how to balance innovation incentives with safeguards against concentration, instability, and erosion of social capital. Education: From a focus on STEM to is college worth it? The digital economy increased the premium to higher education and STEM skills, intensifying the long-running “race between education and technology” (Goldin and Katz 2008). Demand has grown not only for advanced technical expertise but also for complementary skills in problem-solving, communication, and adaptability. Many universities and community colleges shifted their course and degree offerings toward computer science, data analytics, and engineering programs, while online learning platforms have broadened access to technical training. Yet rising tuition costs, unequal K– 12 preparation, and geographic disparities in school quality risk widening skill gaps. Today, a growing number of high school graduates doubt whether a college degree is worth the cost involved. This development is a stark change from the way higher education has been viewed for the better part of a century. records.text: 3 April 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Bond Market Strategy The term premium is at a decade high. But is it too high? No. Some commentators have argued that the UST10Y is cheap because measures of term premia are high relative to recent history. It is factually correct that term premia are close to a decade high. The DB term premium (5s10s slope + 20% short in 2s) has indeed risen from below 50bp in 2022, when we argued that term premia were likely to be on a secular uptrend, to above 100bp today. But that does not mean that the term premium is too high. Indeed, in an environment with persistent negative supply shocks and structurally easier fiscal policy, term premia should increase. During negative supply shocks, bonds are not good hedges for equities as higher inflation is bad for both bonds and equities. As the hedging properties are eroded, bonds should have a higher risk premium. Separately, significant upward pressure on deficits will reduce excess savings and thereby put upward pressure on term premia and equilibrium rates. Bottom line: in an environment where the negative supply shock to oil is persistent and there is very significant latent demand for fiscal policy, it remains more likely that term premia will rise than decline from current levels. The Panic of 1893 similarly reflected overexpansion and rate competition that eroded profitability, leaving many lines insolvent. In both episodes, industrial concentration increased through reorganization, as financiers consolidated distressed assets into larger systems, reinforcing the rise of corporate capitalism (Lamoreaux 1985; Chandler 1977). More broadly, the scale and indivisibility of steam, steel, and rail technologies amplified cyclical volatility. Large fixed costs, network externalities, and expectations of national market integration encouraged rapid expansion during booms and sharp retrenchment during downturns. We interpret the financial panics of the late 19th century as endogenous byproducts of industrialization’s capital intensity and speculative financing, rather than exogenous shocks unrelated to technological change. Following the panics, heavy industry concentrated. Carnegie’s steel operations achieved large economies of scale, while merger waves around 1900 created U.S. Steel under J.P. Morgan. In oil, Standard Oil came to dominate refining through horizontal integration and control of transportation networks (Chandler 1977).

NBER, Morgan Stanley Research Wages, Living Standards, and Inequality: Enter the Gilded Age The age of steam and steel produced substantial gains in productivity and income. By the late 19th century, labor productivity growth approached 2% annually, or about double the rate of the first industrial revolution, leading to a sustained rise in real GDP per capita (Maddison 2001). In the Exhibits below, we find similar results. A simple estimate of real output per person – using either employment data or labor force data – suggests productivity gains of 2.1-2.3% per year in the second half of the 1800s. Railroads broadened access to goods, urban transit improved mobility, and communications technologies compressed economic distance. Yet these gains were unevenly distributed due, in part, to industry concentration and monopoly power. The Gilded Age witnessed extreme wealth concentration, with leading industrialists amassing vast fortunes while many workers faced precarious employment and poor working conditions (Piketty and Saez 2003). Workers Displaced by Technology Face More Difficult Labor Market Transitions Workers displaced from technology-disrupted occupations face more difficult transitions back into employment after losing their jobs. Throughout our analysis, we benchmark their outcomes against workers in “stable” occupations—those in the middle two quartiles of employment growth—and “expanding” occupations—those in the top quartile. Relative to these benchmarks, technology-displaced workers take roughly one month longer to find a new job and suffer real earnings losses 3pp larger upon reemployment when moving between full-time positions (Exhibit 4). These estimates are broadly stable across the two cohorts in our sample and closely aligned with our previous analysis of technological displacement over 1994-2024 using the Current Population Survey’s Displaced Worker Supplement. The NCCBR segment is relatively opaque and not captured by SOFR’s calculation, though it currently makes up a significant proportion of dealers’ lending to hedge funds, most of which occurs at higher rates than the current SOFR distribution. The central clearing mandate is poised to integrate more activity in this segment into the SOFR calculation, which will have the technical impact of biasing SOFR higher toward dealer-hedge fund client trades. The two key effects will be a wider SOFR-fed funds spread (SERFF more negative), and a compression of the GC-SOFR spread. To quantify the potential impact on SOFR, we use data from Office of Financial Research’s (OFR) 2022 NCCBR pilot collection (which captured data for three days in the span of two weeks in June 2022), acknowledging that funding market conditions are vastly different from back then. A research note published by the OFR last year found that central clearing the NCCBR segment would not have shifted SOFR at all in 2022 due to exemptions for repo that would either not need to be cleared, such as those with non-Treasury collateral, or that would not be included in the SOFR calculation, such as term repo (SOFR is overnight only)

records.text: 1. Europe-wide shock: when both the Italian and German sovereign yield curve steepen (10y-2y BTP and 10y-2y Bund) and the Italian sovereign spread (10y BTP-Bund) tightens. 2. Domestic risk: when the Italian sovereign yield curve flattens and the Italian sovereign spread widens. 3. Rates sell-off: when both the Italian and German sovereign yield curve steepen and the Italian sovereign spread widens. In this simple way, it is possible to assess whether the market pricing of Italian sovereign spreads is more likely to be due to external macro factors – e.g. an improved growth outlook in the region, increasing long-end rates but keeping the spread tight – or to risk factors specific to the Italian landscape that increase the long and front end of the yield curve and the sovereign spread at the same time. We find that domestic risk (a flatter Italian curve and wider spread) remains contained, while spread widening is combined with a flatter curve in both Italy and Germany, pointing to rising growth concerns beyond the Italian economy (Exhibit 4). Country-specific risks could become more significant in the future, especially if the energy shock deteriorates. We identify two key factors for the Italian outlook: the scale of the fiscal response to the energy crisis and the rising political risk that could jeopardize the final disbursements and implementation of the European Recovery Fund. While this provides near term relief, it blunts price signals, supports demand, and risks keeping inflation elevated, especially as such measures are typically capped and financed through expenditure reallocation rather than sustained deficit expansion. The trade offs are sharpest for energy importing EMs with limited fiscal space, where broad support can undermine external balances and policy credibility, while energy exporters benefit from improved terms of trade and, in some cases, added fiscal revenue. This divergence helps explain why EM central bank responses remain highly country specific rather than coordinated. Other countries have shifted toward more targeted support, focusing on vulnerable households or specific sectors while allowing energy prices to pass through more fully. Volatile jobs estimates continue to reflect swings in birth-death adjustments As we had emphasized following the previous two employment reports, unusual birth-death adjustments appear to have been a substantial factor behind January's strong and February's weak job gains (Figure 3-Figure 4). records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 23 The Third Wave: Electricity and the Internal Combustion Engine (c. 1890-1950) Diffusion and Organizational Change The third innovation wave, which economic historians generally date from the 1890s through the 1940s, centered on electricity, the internal combustion engine, chemicals, and modern communications. A key feature of the third innovation wave is that the economy- wide effects of some of its main inventions, like Thomas Edison's first commercial power plant (Pearl Street Station) and early gasoline automobiles in the 1890s, manifested only with large-scale diffusion and organizational redesign (David 1990; Gordon 2016). Electrification spread rapidly after 1900 as central generating stations and transmission networks expanded from major cities to smaller towns. Electricity generation increased more than tenfold between 1902 and 1929, reflecting both industrial and household adoption (Gordon 2016). The shift from steam-driven line shafts to decentralized electric motors allowed for more flexible plant layouts and continuous-flow production, raising productivity and facilitating mass production. The internal combustion engine similarly transformed transportation and spatial organization. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 29 The Fourth Wave: Electronics and Aviation (c. 1940-1980) Technological Foundations: A successful public-private partnership The fourth innovation wave, which economic historians generally date from the 1940s through the 1980s, was propelled by advances in electronics, aerospace, and early digital computing. Not surprisingly, many of the innovations that altered the private sector of the US economy during this time period were rooted in World War II mobilization. Federal government spending through research and development outlays during the war and subsequent Cold War accelerated radar, jet propulsion, nuclear engineering, and computing. An important inflection point came in 1947 with the invention of the transistor and subsequent development of integrated circuits. Both laid the foundation for modern electronics. At the same time, commercial jet aviation (for example, the Boeing 707 was released in 1958) dramatically reduced travel times and further increased global integration (Gordon 2016). The Interstate Highway Act of 1956 further reorganized economic geography, facilitated suburbanization, and established long-haul trucking and the seeds of just-in-time logistics. Across the four ISM components, we expect business activity, new orders, and employment weakened in March, while the supplier deliveries component — which often rises when cost and logistical pressures build — likely limited the downside, keeping the composite at 54.0. Note that respondents to the ISM services survey can respond throughout the month, so firms likely had adequate time to digest the Middle East conflict and run-up in fuel prices. records.text: channel to achieving that outcome. Regulatory changes We view last year’s eSLR modification as helping support a higher floor for long-end spreads. We estimate this impact to be around 15-20 bps, basing our assumptions on an average of 12% after-tax return on equity and 1.5% reduced capital charge to GSIBs’ dealer subsidiaries for intermediating in Treasuries. The reproposed GSIB framework this month also supports wider spreads in two ways. First, by eliminating year-end repo volatility and improving overall funding stability. Second, the proposal enhances Treasury dealer capacity by recalibrating the treatment for repo-intensive balance sheets, with banks that rely more on short- term repo funding capturing bigger benefits. These measures support spreads along the full curve. The Basel III proposal could support spreads indirectly if non-dealer banks deploy capital to buy securities, including Treasuries. However, credit demand in the economy may determine whether securities or loans are the larger beneficiary. Valuation We think front-end and belly spreads remain attractive to own, while long-end spreads also look undervalued and positioning is now cleaner. In our fair value models, 2yr spreads appear slightly rich, while 5yr, 10yr and 30yr spreads are broadly in line with levels implied by repo funding, volatility, and Treasury supply- demand dynamics. records.text: US Economics Weekly3 April 2026 ab 29 release noted, "While not obvious in the headline or its component indexes, the weight of rising costs due to tariff pass-through and spiking oil prices was evident among other measures in the survey like inflation expectations ." Consumers' median 12-month inflation expectations rose in March to levels last seen in May 2025, during heightened tariff concerns, up 0.7 pp to 5.2%. The survey period for preliminary results in the Conference Board survey extended from March 1 to March 24, so respondents likely had time to digest the Middle East conflict and the run-up in fuel prices. Labor market assessments were little changed in March. The widely-watched and highly cyclical labor market differential (the difference between the share of respondents reporting jobs as "plentiful" versus "hard to get") rose 0.1 point to 5.8. The share of respondents reporting jobs as "plentiful" rose 0.6 pp to 27.3%, while the share reporting "hard to get" rose 0.5 pp to 21.5% in March. Both the share reporting jobs as plentiful and as hard to get are back to around 2016 and 2017 levels. The share of respondents expecting less employment six months hence rose 1.7 pp to 27.9%, remaining elevated, as expectations for the labor market across surveys remains quite weak. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Navigating the Final Inning(s) of This Correction Our views have been consistent on several fronts since the conflict started. First, we have contended that the probability of this oil spike ending the business cycle in the US is low given that earnings growth is accelerating and positive today, whereas it was decelerating and negative in historical periods where a surge in crude prices caused a recession. In addition, the magnitude of the move in crude today in year-over-year terms is still below what it was in those historical episodes. Not to mention, when adjusted for gold, the real price of oil is lower than other energy shocks. The US is also less vulnerable than other nations to a rise in energy costs, particularly natural gas. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, we remain convicted in our out of consensus view that the US already experienced a labor cycle in the private economy between 2022-2025. In our view, Liberation Day and DOGE firings last year marked the culmination of this rolling recession, the rate of change trough on the overall labor market and the start of a rolling recovery/ early cycle backdrop which we think continues to gain momentum despite the recent headwinds. The resiliency of the ISM Manufacturing survey for March (above consensus at 52.7), released last week, and the acceleration in RevPAR per our Gaming, Lodging & Leisure analyst Stephen Grambling, support our claim. records.text: US Economics Weekly 03 April 2026 Citi Research 2 Developments affecting energy prices continue to be the dominant force driving global markets despite more economic data released this week. Even market reactions to a very strong 178k jobs added in March were somewhat muted, with 2- year Treasury yields moving around 5bp higher. Oil prices rose as the specifics on a path towards resolution of Middle East disruptions remain unclear. But rather than a substantial move higher in yields on concerns of higher inflation, interest rate markets have shifted more towards balancing downward growth implications from higher oil prices with upside inflation risks. Fed officials will feel very comfortable keeping rates on hold for now following the strong March jobs report, with markets pricing rates essentially unchanged through the year. We continue to think signs of a weakening labor market will result in cuts later in the year. But timing of upcoming data suggest a later start to rate cuts than we had previously been expecting. We now expect 75bp of cuts this year starting in September (September, October, and December meetings), also a very similar pattern to recent years. One of these considerations is the impact on dealer intermediation capacity, with the OFR estimating that central clearing would have netted over $200bn in repo positions in August last year. During periods of heightened demand for balance sheet netting, such as month- and quarter-ends, dealers push clients into centrally cleared repo activity. However, this introduces RWA capital constraints for some banks, as the dominant sponsored central clearing service (in which dealers sponsor clients into FICC) requires dealers to guarantee the performance of the sponsored member. These constraints contribute to persistent intermediation challenges in sensitive periods within the current repo market structure. Conclusion Based on available information, we anticipate only a modest increase in SOFR, approximately 1-2bps, as a result of the shift to central clearing given the offsetting effects of the mechanical rise from incorporating higher-rate repos and the reduction in intermediation and balance sheet constraints. There are a number of other relevant factors that could swing the clearing mandate’s impact on SOFR in either direction. For instance, whether the combination of cross-margining, ACS access model development, and “done-away” development can effectively reduce the higher costs (both margin and operational) associated with central clearing. If costs are brought down, relative value trades would be more attractive, increasing leverage demand and consequently, funding rates. Conversely, ongoing liquidity and capital deregulation for large banks could stimulate increased bank lending into repo, which would keep a tighter lid on SOFR despite higher leverage demand. Finally, industry representatives have requested additional exemptions from central clearing for foreign financial institutions, and given that many hedge funds engaging in fixed-income relative value trades are domiciled in the Cayman Islands, such exemptions could materially reduce the volume of NCCBR activity subject to the mandate. records.text: M Foundation 20 This rapid economic expansion contributed to financial excess and periodic crashes, including the Panics of 1873 and 1893, both closely linked to railroad overbuilding and fragile financing (Kindleberger and Aliber 2005; Romer 1989). These crises were not incidental to industrialization, but they were tightly connected to the financial architecture of the second innovation wave. Railroads were the largest capital-intensive enterprises of the era, requiring unprecedented fixed investment in track, rolling stock, and terminals. From 1872-1881, railroad investment averaged 2.5% of GDP – about $790bn in current dollars – and railroad investment was routinely 10% or more of gross capital formation (Cootner 1963). If there is any historical antecedent to the burgeoning AI-spending story, it is railroad- related investment. Financing relied heavily on bond issuance marketed domestically and in Europe, often backed by optimistic projections of westward settlement and freight demand (Fogel 1964; Chandler 1977). When traffic revenues failed to meet expectations or foreign capital flows reversed, highly leveraged railroad balance sheets proved vulnerable. The Panic of 1873 followed the failure of Jay Cooke & Co., a major underwriter of Northern Pacific bonds, triggering widespread railroad bankruptcies and a prolonged contraction. records.text: separate signal from noise. Why Use the Current Population Survey to Understand the Effects of AI on Labor? The Current Population Survey (CPS) is the primary household survey used to measure US labor market conditions. The survey is conducted jointly by the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics and samples roughly 60,000 households every month (since 1940). The CPS is designed to be representative of the civilian noninstitutional population and its purpose is to produce the official statistics on employment, unemployment, and labor force participation, including the U3 unemployment rate. The CPS collects detailed labor force information on individuals age 16 and over, classifying them as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. For those employed, it gathers data on hours worked, industry, occupation, class of worker (wage and salaried or self-employed), and part-time vs. full-time status. For those classified as unemployed, it records duration of unemployment, job search activities, and reasons for unemployment. The survey also captures other key demographic characteristics — including age, sex, race, ethnicity, education, and family status — which allow for disaggregated labor market analysis. Overall, the CPS is useful for understanding the effects of AI on the labor market since it provides high-frequency, nationally representative data with consistent definitions over time. records.text: 3 April 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 15 Return of leverage demand? Andrew Fu | Strategist | +1-212-250-1743 As we noted last month, the Treasury basis trade’s profitability has compressed and positions have lightened since the start of the year. This can be partly attributed to a slowdown in asset managers’ accumulation of Treasury futures, as the cash - futures basis fundamentally stems from excess investor demand for futures relative to cash Treasuries. In today’s chart, we show how in the last decade, asset manager demand for futures is driven in part by the difference in duration between the Bloomberg US Agg benchmark (Agg) as a whole and its Treasuries component. This difference comes mostly from the duration of the MBS component of the Agg, which is sensitive to the level of interest rates given how MBS duration extends when mortgage prepayments slow in higher rate environments. The strong correlation between index duration differences and the following year’s asset manager futures positions makes sense for several reasons. Previous Fed research found that asset managers utilize futures both as a source of leverage and as a way to manage duration. Futures free up cash for asset managers to deploy into credit products yielding a spread above Treasuries, which improves the probability of outperforming the benchmark in most market conditions. records.text: Lessons for AI-driven Occupational Displacement Our analysis suggests that, similarly to previous waves of technological change, AI-driven displacement could impose lasting costs on affected workers, worsening labor market outcomes for several years. These effects could be substantially larger when displacement coincides with a recession. However, even if AI-driven job losses disproportionately affect new graduates, our findings suggest that younger workers will likely find it easier to adjust by switching jobs and upgrading skills. And encouragingly, our analysis suggests that retraining programs could help to mitigate some of the negative effects of AI-related job displacement, enabling displaced workers to earn modestly higher wages and achieve more stable employment. These mitigating strategies face challenges should energy prices stay higher for longer. If Brent oil prices in aggregate rise and remain around US$120/bbl with natural gas around US$30/mm BTU, Asia’s oil and gas burden would rise to 6.5% of GDP – the historical peaks where growth downside intensifies and demand destruction begins (physical cargoes are being traded at much higher prices than what most investors are used to tracking). Our rule of thumb is that each sustained US$10 increase in oil prices reduces Asia’s GDP growth by ~20-30bp on a gross basis, or ~10-15bp after mitigating measures and fiscal offsets. The burden is uneven across the region: Thailand, Korea, Taiwan, India, and Japan are more exposed while China is relatively better placed. Fortunately, inflation in most of Asia is relatively benign. That gives central banks some room to maneuver before macro stability risks are stretched to the point where they must hike. If oil prices stay at US$110/bbl for three months but move back to US$80/bbl, we don’t expect central banks in Asia to raise rates except the BOJ, for which we forecast a hike before geopolitical tensions began. records.text: 4. The Scarring Effects of Technological Displacement Are Larger in Recessions Recessions significantly amplify the costs of technological displacement for affected workers. As we noted in previous reports, firms disproportionately shed routine jobs during downturns, when they are under greater pressure to identify efficiencies and streamline their workforce. For individual workers, technology-induced displacement during a recession amplifies the labor market penalty already faced relative to workers displaced from other occupations. The baseline gaps estimated during expansions widen further during recessions—by about three weeks for the duration of unemployment spells and 5pp each for the risk of subsequent unemployment and the probability of exiting the labor force entirely (Exhibit 11). This likely reflects the fact that reemployment becomes harder and job matches less durable when many displaced workers compete for a limited number of vacancies in occupations that are rapidly contracting. records.text: 3 April 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 8 Deutsche Bank AG Examining the impact of central clearing on SOFR and repo With the deadline for the SEC central clearing mandate of eligible UST repo trades a little over a year out (June 2027), regulators have been working to facilitate development of requisite infrastructure to ensure that the costs associated with the transition are minimized. Central clearing promises to reduce systemic risks and enhance dealer balance sheet efficiency, though not without raising specific industry concerns, including higher costs associated with clearing trades to a central counterparty (CCP), imposed on both the margin and capital fronts. The details around how these issues are addressed will determine the full impact on funding markets. In this note, we focus specifically on how the transition might impact SOFR fixings within the Fed’s target range. Adding a new segment to SOFR The prevailing repo market structure continues to favor the non-centrally cleared bilateral repo (NCCBR) segment despite the benefits that central clearing offers, such as mitigated counterparty risks and balance sheet netting for dealers. This preference stems from the additional legal and operational costs associated with central clearing, alongside the required margins calculated via strict Value-at-Risk (VaR) models imposed by the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation (FICC). records.text: The Long-Run Effects of Technological Disruption on Workers The rapid advance of artificial intelligence (AI) has deepened concerns about its potential to disrupt—or even eliminate—entire occupations. Our Global Economics team estimated that AI could displace 6–7% of US workers over the next decade, raising the unemployment rate by up to ½pp relative to trend during a ten-year transition period, with larger unemployment rate increases if the adoption timeline is compressed. Many workers will benefit from AI-driven increases in productivity and real income. But how costly is technological disruption for workers who are displaced? In this week’s Analyst, we draw on four decades of individual-level data from the National Longitudinal Surveys to assess the short- and long-term “scarring” effects of technological disruption on US workers. Identifying Technology-Disrupted Occupations We identify technology-disrupted occupations by analyzing employment trends across more than 300 occupation categories in the American Community Survey since the 1980s. Occupations with high routine task intensity—a measure developed by economist David Autor and co-authors1 to capture the degree to which jobs involve routine, codifiable tasks rather than abstract cognitive work or non-routine manual dexterity—experienced significantly weaker employment growth across recent decades, consistent with their greater exposure to automation (Exhibit 1). Evidence That AI May Be Changing Tasks Within Jobs There is wide consensus that the adoption of generative AI will, at a minimum, alter the tasks workers perform across occupations. If GenAI ultimately transforms labor markets, one would expect to observe signs of either task augmentation or displacement, alongside evidence of AI adoption and changing occupational tasks. The open question is how quickly firms are adopting these technologies and translating them into changes in production processes. CPS data provide evidence that AI may already be affecting job tasks. Because the CPS follows individuals over time, it allows us to track whether workers report changes in their work activities. Importantly, however, observed task changes do not necessarily reflect shifts in production processes: workers may report different tasks because they change jobs or move across occupations. records.text: Retraining also helps to cushion the impact of displacement. The National Longitudinal Surveys provide information on whether respondents participated in vocational or technical programs, apprenticeships, government-sponsored initiatives, or employer-provided training between survey waves. To estimate the effect of these programs, we again apply a propensity score matching approach, comparing technology-displaced workers who spent at least four weeks in retraining within three years of a job loss with otherwise comparable technology-displaced workers who did not participate. We find that retrained workers achieve roughly 2pp more cumulative real wage growth over the decade following displacement, and their probability of returning to unemployment at least once during that period declines by about 10pp (Exhibit 9). These gains reflect skill upgrading relative to other technology-displaced workers. Retrained workers tend to move up the occupational ladder into roles with higher abstract content—positions requiring advanced skills and greater complementarity with information and communication technology—thereby reducing their exposure to future automation (Exhibit 10, left panel). They also tend to transition into roles with higher complexity scores as measured by the BLS’s National Compensation Survey (Exhibit 10, right panel). The canal boom of the 1820s and 1830s produced many unsuccessful ventures. Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois undertook ambitious programs financed by heavy borrowing. Pennsylvania’s Main Line of Public Works and the Illinois and Michigan Canal, for example, imposed large fiscal burdens and contributed to state debt crises after 1837 (Goodrich 1960; Wallis 2000). Not all early infrastructure projects failed, however. The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, was successful, sharply reducing transport costs and generating toll revenues that exceeded construction costs (North 1961; Goodrich 1960). In the United States, craft workers in the 1820s and 1830s organized early trade unions and citywide labor associations, pressing for shorter hours and higher wages and encountering adverse judicial rulings (Wilentz 1984). These responses illustrate a recurring pattern: technological change raises aggregate productivity while redistributing income across skills and sectors. At the same time, demographic and geographic adjustment accelerated. The US population nearly quadrupled between 1800 and 1850, and the urban share rose from roughly 6 percent to 20 percent by 1860 (Carter et al. 2006). Urbanization generated economies of scale that still exist today, but also congestion costs, prompting municipal public health and sanitation reforms. Contemporary observers such as Tocqueville noted widening disparities between industrial wealth and wage labor, highlighting concerns about inequality, child labor, and concentrated economic power (Tocqueville 1835). These distributional tensions foreshadowed the more organized labor and agrarian political movements of the later 19th century. Historically, oil price increases mainly affect headline inflation rather than core. As noted in a recent piece, our models suggest that a 10% rise in oil prices is consistent with a roughly 35bp boost to headline inflation, but only about a 3bp increase in core. As we noted last month, the Treasury basis trade’s profitability has compressed and positions have lightened since the start of the year. This can be partly attributed to a slowdown in asset managers’ accumulation of Treasury futures, as the cash- futures basis fundamentally stems from excess investor demand for futures relative to cash Treasuries. In today’s chart, we show how in the last decade, asset manager demand for futures is driven in part by the difference in duration between the Bloomberg US Agg benchmark (Agg) as a whole and its Treasuries component. This difference comes mostly from the duration of the MBS component of the Agg, which is sensitive to the level of interest rates given how MBS duration extends when mortgage prepayments slow in higher rate environments. The strong correlation between index duration differences and the following year’s asset manager futures positions makes sense for several reasons. Previous Fed research found that asset managers utilize futures both as a source of leverage and as a way to manage duration. Futures free up cash for asset managers to deploy into credit products yielding a spread above Treasuries, which improves the probability of outperforming the benchmark in most market conditions. records.text: 2 Canada Viewpoint | 06 April 2026 BoC on hold despite higher oil prices We think the bar for the BoC to hike rates this year is quite high, and our baseline is that the BoC will remain on hold for the foreseeable future with the policy rate at 2.25%. If the Iran conflict escalates and oil prices remain above $100/bbl for several weeks, the probability of a hike rises —but so does the probability of a global recession, which would increase the odds that the BoC ultimately has to cut. Macro conditions argue for patience The Canadian economy is weak We recently raised our GDP growth forecasts to 1.2% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027 to reflect the impact of higher oil prices (see our Global Economic Viewpoint). Canada’s status as a net energy exporter —with an energy trade surplus near 3% of GDP— supports activity even as the broader economy remains soft amid uncertainty and weaker global growth (Exhibit 1). Still, growth is below potential, impacted by trade uncertainty given US tariffs and the incoming USMCA review, so we continue to estimate a negative output gap in 2026 (Exhibit 2-Exhibit 3). Upside risks stem from the government’s fiscal impulse: higher oil prices likely enable more spending, though we assume no change to the fiscal deficit. Temporary higher growth could also come from the FIFA World Cup. Common Themes Across the Five Innovation Waves Across 250 years of American economic history, each innovation wave fundamentally reorganized the structure of the economy. The first two waves pulled the country out of its agrarian roots and into an industrially integrated economy, connecting regional markets through canals and railroads. Electrification and motorization then enabled mass production and national consumer markets. Electronics and aviation shifted the economy toward services and science-based industry. The digital revolution completed the transition from an agrarian to industrial to knowledge-based economy built on networks and intangible capital. Each wave did more than introduce new tools: it rewired how the economy functioned, where people lived, how firms organized production, and how value was created. These transformations were powered by extraordinary surges in capital spending. Innovation waves are never incremental; they have been correlated with investment booms. Canal construction absorbed roughly 1% of GDP at its peak, while railroads commanded up to 2–3% of GDP annually and more than 10% of gross capital formation. In recent price action, a transition is starting to take shape in how markets trade oil rallies. Previously, the primary focus was on inflation concerns, contributing to a significant surge in front-end yields (especially in Europe) that provided some relative insulation to FX. Now, there appears to be a shift toward pricing in the downside risks to global growth. This is consistent with our prior analysis which found that the pivot from inflation to growth typically comes two to six weeks after oil prices peak. That said, this historical analysis relies on having an ex-post sense of confidence that energy prices have peaked , which cannot be said for now. Macroeconomic data thus far does suggest some softening in demand, though signals of rapid deterioration are absent. This is while recent inflation prints continue to underscore the upside risks from the energy rally. As a result, it is not particularly obvious why the narrative has shifted, but we would we would point toward two key factors: 1) pre-war energy supply buffers have been exhausted, indicating that any floor for prices is rising and staying higher for longer is more likely, and 2) news flow out of energy importers in Asia is highlighting vulnerabilities to this sustained shock. Median one-year ahead inflation expectations rose 0.4 pp to 3.8%, partially retracing to the 4.0% level in January. Since 1993, a one-dollar increase in the all-grade average US retail gasoline price from the EIA over a month has been associated with a 0.7-pp increase in University of Michigan one-year ahead inflation expectations over a month. The all- grade average US retail gasoline price sat at $4.13 in the last week of March, up $1.05 since the last week of February. Thus, at least in the March data, one-year ahead inflation expectations rose slightly less than historical relationships would imply, but the series may move further up in the April data. Consumers remain concerned about the labor market in the University of Michigan survey. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. records.text: M Foundation 4 era saw federal R&D quadruple as a share of GDP. The digital age redirected investment from factories and structures toward software, computing equipment, and intellectual property. Every wave demanded heavy, front-loaded capital deepening, with early waves focusing on physical capital and structures and later waves on computers, peripherals, and software. The technologies were capital-intensive, network-based, and financed by optimistic projections of permanent growth. Labor markets were never spared, though innovation largely complemented employment. As we have previously written about, each innovation wave displaced existing occupations and reshuffled skill demand. The first industrial revolution reduced the role of artisans and expanded semi-skilled factory labor. The railroad and steel era accelerated urbanization and created the modern managerial class. Electrification further reduced farm employment and expanded clerical and professional work. Postwar electronics and aerospace strengthened technical occupations while manufacturing employment peaked and then began to decline. The digital revolution hollowed out middle-skill routine jobs, pushing employment toward high-skill professional roles and lower-wage services. Yet across all five waves, the total demand for labor did not collapse. Workers were reallocated rather than rendered obsolete. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 9 first industrial revolution to 1793, when Samuel Slater built the first successful cotton- spinning mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. Over the span of about 50 years, American entrepreneurs adapted and improved British innovations to suit local conditions, laying the groundwork for industrialization. The period from approximately the 1790s through the 1840s saw the spread of steam power and factory-based manufacturing, although progress was gradual at first. Early factories relied heavily on water power and thus clustered in river-based regions of the Northeast (Atack et. al. 1980). The first U.S. railroads also appeared during this era, heralding a new age of steam- powered transportation. By 1830, just one year after Britain’s first railway, the United States had 23 miles of rail track, which surged to over 2,800 miles by 1840. Taken together, innovations in textiles, high-pressure steam engines, canals and railroads, and iron-making defined the initial industrial revolution in America. Researchers Sam Manning and Tomas Aguirre argue that the employees in the most AI- exposed sectors might have the most applicable skills to transfer to other sectors and roles. We reproduced their scatterplot of "vulnerability" above. "We find that AI exposure and adaptive capacity are positively correlated: many occupations highly exposed to AI contain workers with relatively strong means to manage a job transition. Of the 34.7 million workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 23.9 million also have above-median adaptive capacity, leaving them comparatively well-equipped to handle job transitions if displacement occurs. At the same time, 3.3 million workers (2.5 percent of the workforce in our sample) are both highly exposed and have low adaptive capacity. These workers are concentrated in clerical, administrative support, and assistance roles. Importantly, AI exposure reflects potential changes to work tasks, not inevitable displacement; only some of the changes brought on by AI will result in job loss. By distinguishing between highly exposed workers with relatively strong means to adjust and those with limited adaptive capacity, our analysis shows that exposure measures alone can obscure both areas of resilience to technological change and concentrated pockets of vulnerability if displacement were to occur." Unlike in 2022, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz could result in a physical lack of energy availability, especially for Asia, which sources over 50% of its crude and more than a third of its gas via the strait (Figure 3A s i a d e p e n d e n c y o n o i l f l o w s t h r o u g h H o r m u z a n d d a y s o f i n v e n t o r y c o v e r ). If the strait remains closed for a prolonged period, the region could face outright shortages, which could curtail economic activity in a manner reminiscent of COVID-era restrictions where businesses shut down and workers were let go, leading to hard-to-reverse economic scarring (see Asian central bank dilemma: 2020 versus 2022, Sajjid Chinoy, 27 Mar). Much like during COVID, the shock unfolds sequentially rather than simultaneously a rolling supply disruption moving westward, dictated by shipping times and buffered unevenly by regional inventories. The COVID shock was primarily a demand shock, with lockdowns and mobility restrictions leading to a collapse in consumption and services. The Iran conflict, by contrast, is primarily a supply shock, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupting the physical flow of energy and other key commodities. However, if the supply shock is severe enough to cause actual shortages, it could trigger a demand collapse similar to COVID, especially in energy- dependent economies. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 35 The Fifth Wave: The Internet and Digital Networks (c. 1990- 2020) Core Technologies and Duration The fifth innovation wave, beginning in the early 1990s, is organized around digital networks, computing power, and data. The commercialization of the internet, broadband diffusion, mobile computing, and cloud infrastructure dramatically lowered the cost of storing, processing, and transmitting information. Advances in semiconductors and software expanded the scope of automation beyond routine manual tasks to include cognitive and analytical functions (Brynjolfsson and McAfee 2014; Autor 2015). The steady decline in computing costs—often summarized by Moore’s Law—enabled exponential growth in data storage and processing capacity, fostering new applications in finance, logistics, healthcare, and media (Tevlin and Whelan 2003). As in earlier waves, the largest gains required complementary organizational change—platform architectures, supply-chain digitization, data analytics integration, and new business models built around user networks and algorithmic matching. Firms that successfully reorganized around digital technologies realized outsized productivity and market-share gains, reinforcing divergence across industries and companies. Even during severe downturns, there is no evidence that technological progress permanently raised the natural rate of unemployment. The composition of work changed; work itself endured. Productivity growth is the ultimate signature of these waves. Early diffusion is often slow and uneven, but once complementary investments and organizational change take hold, output per worker accelerates. The first industrial revolution generated modest but rising gains. The steam and steel era doubled productivity growth rates relative to the prior century. Electrification and motorization produced the “Great Leap” of the early 20th century, doubling output per hour in a generation. The postwar period delivered one of the strongest sustained productivity expansions in U.S. history. The internet wave produced a sharp acceleration in the late 1990s, even if gains later moderated. Across waves, productivity surges are real, but they require time, diffusion, and structural adaptation. Macroeconomic volatility and boom-bust cycles are not accidents of innovation, they are necessary companions. The canal boom collapsed in 1837. Railroad overbuilding fueled the panics of 1873 and 1893. The electrification era encompassed the Great Depression. The late 1990s tech boom ended in a dramatic equity collapse. records.text: Breaking Down the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Substitution vs. Augmentation We have previously used a measure of how exposed an occupation’s work activities are to artificial intelligence to track AI’s impact on the labor market. In today’s US Daily, we delve deeper by distinguishing between two distinct channels of the AI impact: substitution and augmentation. In occupations where AI is likely to substitute for human labor, the impact on employment is likely negative, as firms deploy AI to automate tasks once handled by humans. In occupations where AI augments human labor, the impact is more ambiguous: AI augmentation that makes workers more productive can reduce the number of workers needed to produce a fixed amount of output, but by lowering the cost per unit of output it might also increase demand for what they produce enough to generate a net increase in their employment (the so-called Jevons paradox). Disentangling these two channels empirically is difficult. Many widely used AI exposure indices capture only the overlap between existing AI capabilities and the human abilities required for a given occupation. By construction, these indices are agnostic about whether AI serves as a substitute or complement for human labor (Exhibit 1). records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 9 Micro Data May Show Incipient Disruption At face value, the Current Population Survey (CPS), which tracks individuals, does not yield clear evidence of AI-related disruption. This is not surprising given the broader “no- hire/no-fire” environment, which does not align naturally with a disruption narrative. The CPS underlies the BLS household survey measures and labor market flows. CPS data are not seasonally adjusted, so we focus on 12-month moving averages to smooth seasonality and other high-frequency noise. However, controlling for differences in occupational cyclicality and focusing on young workers can reveal potential early signals. Comparisons across degrees of AI exposure help reduce the noise, but they should not be interpreted as definitive evidence. This analysis suffers from an "omitted variables problem" in econometrics parlance. Put differently, other shocks — such as monetary policy, tariffs, or immigration policy changes — may also affect occupations differently. Post-Covid hiring trends across different industries, which could be unrelated to AI, may also be playing a role; for example, tech had higher turnover post-Covid and slower hiring now. A persistent pattern that strengthens as AI adoption increases will be needed to separate signal from noise. Why Use the Current Population Survey to Understand the Effects of AI on Labor? Manufacturing employment continued to decline sharply after 2000, reflecting a combination of automation and import competition (Autor, Dorn, and Hanson 2013). Others point to the ascension of China into the WTO and hyperglobalization as fueling these trends. At the same time, new occupations—software development, data science, cybersecurity, digital marketing, logistics management, and platform-based gig work—expanded rapidly, illustrating the ongoing reallocation of tasks rather than a net disappearance of work, as we wrote about here. Geographic disparities widened as technology hubs attracted high- skill workers and capital, while regions reliant on routine manufacturing faced persistent adjustment costs. In Exhibit 51 below we plot the change in employment according to internet-digital exposure from 1983 to 2007. We ranked occupations by their "routineness" and put occupations into three categories: high exposure to internet-digital automation, medium exposure, and low exposure and indexed employment in each group such that 1990 = 100. Growth in employment in low- and medium-exposure occupations outpaced that of high- exposure occupations. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 7 What if History Doesn't Rhyme? The goal of this report was to find commonalities across innovation waves that could provide insight into today's environment, but we acknowledge that this time could be different. As mentioned above, diffusion timelines have been accelerating, and faster AI adoption could lead to more disruption than in the past. Others have cited that AI could have a unique breadth across industries given it is considered a general-purpose technology. In the extreme, If AI is indeed different, then it may substitute for labor rather than augment it (Korninek 2024, Korinek and Stiglitz 2021, Trammell and Korinek 2023). In this scenario, productivity could accelerate as it automates both production and innovation, large-scale displacement of labor could occur, and education would shift toward continuos re-skilling. Rather than experience standard business cycles, the economy could experience a regime shift to higher growth while inequality sharply increases from a falling labor share. We do not rule out that AI could defy historical precedents and create more extreme outcomes. That said, we think history is a good guide in helping us form baseline expectations of what is to come while acknowledging potential risk scenarios as well.

Conclusion Based on available information, we anticipate only a modest increase in SOFR, approximately 1 -2bps, as a result of the shift to central clearing given the offsetting effects of the mechanical rise from incorporating higher-rate repos and the reduction in i ntermediation and balance sheet constraints. There are a number of other relevant factors that could swing the clearing mandate’s impact on SOFR in either direction. For instance, whether the combination of cross - margining, ACS access model development, an d “done-away” development can effectively reduce the higher costs (both margin and operational) associated with central clearing. If costs are brought down, relative value trades would be more attractive, increasing leverage demand and consequently, funding rates. Conversely, ongoing liquidity and capital deregulation for large banks could stimulate increased bank lending into repo, which would keep a tighter lid on SOFR despite higher leverage demand. records.text: M Global Idea Sunday Start | What's Next in Global Macro The Face-Off for Asia: Energy Prices v Industrial Cycle Morgan Stanley Asia Limited Chetan Ahya Chief Asia Economist Chetan.Ahya@morganstanley.com +852 2239-7812 Geopolitical tensions pose significant challenges to Asia through higher energy prices and natural gas constraints that could disrupt production and exports. But if tensions ease and oil prices start to retrace, we think the industrial cycle in Asia will roar back to life. What happens to production in Asia will be a harbinger for the global economy. Asia is the region most exposed to higher oil and gas prices. Its oil and gas trade balance sits at -2.1% of GDP, above -1.5% for the euro area, while the US is not a net importer of oil and gas. With past oil price spikes, analysis has focused on how well economies can weather higher oil prices. This time around, we must also consider potential supply shortages. Policy makers across the region are using a mix of subsidies, tax adjustments, and other forms of price smoothing to cushion the blow to households and corporates. The pass-through from international oil prices to domestic fuel prices is ~35%. Work-from-home, rationing of select products, and policy guidance to encourage fuel saving have also been deployed. Most Asian economies can use coal to replace the electricity-generating capacity lost from supply constraints to natural gas. These mitigating strategies face challenges should energy prices stay higher

records.text: ssed the Great Depression. The late 1990s tech boom ended in a dramatic equity collapse. Each wave exhibited a similar pattern: exuberant capital formation, speculative financing, rising leverage, and eventual retrenchment. Financial markets both accelerate technological diffusion and amplify the cycle when expectations adjust. Innovation waves have repeatedly contained at least one major boom-bust episode. As Milton Friedman might say, "there is no free lunch." Politics reshapes itself around these disruptions. Industrialization produced early labor organization and Progressive Era reforms. The Gilded Age’s concentration of wealth triggered antitrust and income tax legislation. The third wave produced the New Deal and labor protections. The fourth wave’s prosperity supported a mid-century social compact before later deregulation. The digital era has reopened debates about antitrust, data governance, and market concentration. Technological change consistently redistributes income and power, and political institutions eventually respond. Often slowly, sometimes dramatically.

In Britain, mechanization reduced the number of handloom weavers from roughly 250,000 around 1800 to fewer than 10,000 by mid- century, and a similar process occurred in the US (Allen 2009). Crafts like shoemaking, furniture-making, and metalworking faced increasing competition from factory output. In aggregate, however, industrialization created jobs even as it destroyed others. In other words, innovation caused a churn in labor markets, but labor demand did not evaporate. Instead, employers demanded different skillsets than before. Employment opportunities grew in urban mills, tool shops, ironworks, rail yards, and coal mines, largely drawing labor from agriculture. To meet the rising demand for labor, Immigration accelerated (it played a greater role during the second innovation wave), with many seeking and finding work in industrializing cities (Carter et al. 2006). This first wave of mechanization thus initiated America’s century-long transition from an agricultural to an urban-industrial labor force. records.text: M Foundation 22 Companies Are Increasingly Discussing AI in the Context of Labor Nick Lentini Roughly 12% of S&P 500 companies and 17% of identified AI Adopters referenced labor in relation to AI in transcripts of recent earnings discussions.3 While productivity and efficiency have long been associated with AI adoption (see US Equity Strategy: What Are Companies Saying?), references to labor impacts have risen notably in the most recent quarter. This shift reflects growing investor attention to the potential effects of AI on the labor market, particularly the possibility that AI-driven automation could displace jobs. Markets have generally rewarded companies for cutting costs and linking those reductions — either directly or indirectly — to AI-driven productivity gains. As a result, management teams have a clear incentive to highlight AI-related efficiency stories (see our latest on AI Disruption and TMT Conference takeways). In our experience, positive developments tend to appear earlier in company transcripts, as executives are eager to share them, whereas negative developments — such as layoffs due to slowing business conditions, higher-than-expected costs, or weak demand — often surface with a lag or in retrospect. Given that AI-driven displacement is currently viewed favorably by the market, our view is that the efficiency narrative is likely to persist. records.text: As the last tankers that crossed the Strait of Hormuz before the war are reaching n their destination, concerns about potential oil shortages are rising. We analyze country-product-specific oil markets, identify pockets of potential extreme tightness, and discuss the potential evolution of near-term shortages if the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed for longer. Our three-way analysis highlights already critically low supplies of petrochemical feedstocks — naphtha and LPG — in Asia, with cross-product scarcity in multiple Asian countries in April (Exhibit 1). Approach #1: Products supplied. We analyze country-product specific hits to n supplies/stocks from the Hormuz shock by looking at 1) initial refined products stocks before the conflict; 2) products and crude imports from the Persian Gulf; 3) potential buffers from refining domestic crude stocks, imports from the rest of the world, and export curbs (Exhibit 2). While comprehensive refined products stocks data are not available in all a. countries, Asia countries ex China with available data typically report somewhat lower pre-shock refined oil products stocks, with average products stocks in days of demand at about one month (vs. 50 days in Europe). Stocks also tend to be lower for naphtha and LPG, likely reflecting their more complex storage requirements (Exhibit 3). Asian countries in our sample (accounting for 1/3 of global refined b. products demand) typically source about ½ of their refined products supplies

records.text: US Economic Presentation6 April 2026 ab 25 Source: BLS, BEA, Federal Reserve, Haver, UBS • The FOMC is in a tough spot. No one wants the losses of a labor market contraction, and everyone wants inflation to get to 2.0%. The funds rate can not do much to stop tariff cost-push inflation, but it can risk making a weak labor market too weak. The same goes for energy prices, a rising downside risk to the labor market expansion. Recall the age- old central banker adage “do no harm.” • Tension in the mandate raises the prospect of more dissents. The nominee Kevin Warsh could find a divided FOMC to navigate as a new Chair. • The FOMC pivoted off the weak labor market to deliver three 25 bp rate cuts in 2025, leaving the target range for the funds rate at 3.50% to 3.75%. We expect two 25 bp rate cuts in 2026, with risk of one. The reaction function under a new Chair raises uncertainty and risks around that projection. We also expect higher energy prices are a two- sided risk to the path of policy, not one-sided. records.text: Italy—Growth Slows, Not Stalls; Fiscal Risk Builds, Not Breaks Under the baseline of the conflict in the Middle East extending until the middle of April, we downgraded our European forecasts, lowering Italian GDP growth to 0.5% and 0.6% in 2026 and 2027 (vs 0.9% in both years before the conflict). Consumer confidence and high frequency indicators summarized in our GDP tracker point to additional weakening for economic activity. Since the onset of the Middle East conflict, Italian sovereign bonds have led the widening in Euro area spreads (Exhibit 1). Despite Solid Starting Point, Further Weakening Likely Ahead The recent weakening in economic activity starts from a position of strength. The Italian labour market remains close to the tightest level in 20 years and the employment rate at record highs. But a closer look at employment dynamics suggests that room for additional improvement is now very limited. Almost all the progress of the last 12 years has been as a result of increased labour market participation among the over-50s, with some limited additional contribution from the under-35s and a steady decline in employment for middle-aged individuals (Exhibit 2). Put differently, it is worth considering the implications of not another sharp spike in energy prices, but rather a persistently higher level of oil prices with little if any mean reversion. One key point is that while energy price inflation would arithmetically step down after prices stop rising, second round effects are likely to prove much more persistent than history would suggest. In past oil shocks, prices not only stopped rising, they retraced fairly quickly, helping to cap the duration of pass through. With limited or no reversion for an extended period, firms face a longer lasting cost shock with waning ability to absorb the costs in margins. Inflation risks therefore remain skewed to the upside even as headline prints improve. Exhibit 1: Physical crude oil prices likely reflect tightness in energy supply better than futures. Although the economy went through historically large swings, the third innovation wave did not alter the basic matching characteristics of the labor market: those unemployed for cyclical reasons were able to find re-employment over time. 2. The Wagner Act (1935), formally known as the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), was a cornerstone New Deal law that fundamentally reshaped labor relations in the United States. It guaranteed workers the right to unionize and engage in collective bargaining, prohibited unfair labor practices by employers, such as firing workers for organizing or interfering with union activity, and created the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to enforce labor law and oversee union elections. The Act shifted the legal balance toward labor, leading to a rapid expansion of union membership, particularly in mass-production industries like autos, steel, and electrical manufacturing. Unionization rose sharply after 1935, contributing to higher wages, more stable employment contracts, and the mid-20th-century “Great Compression” in income inequality (Goldin and Margo 1992).

records.text: To explore how these two channels have shaped the recent US labor market, we draw on an occupation-level AI complementarity index developed by IMF economists Pizzinelli, Panton, Tavares, Cazzaniga, and Li (2023).2 This index is constructed based on six critical work abilities from O*NET: (1) interpersonal interaction; (2) accountability; (3) physical proximity; (4) human judgement; (5) share of unstructured work tasks; and (6) level of expertise required to perform work tasks effectively. Occupations receive a lower complementarity score when there is less reliance on face-to-face communication, personal accountability for outcomes, physical presence, frequent judgement calls, unstructured tasks, or specialized expertise. Exhibit 2 illustrates how occupations with similar AI exposure can differ in their degree of AI complementarity. For example, customer service representatives and interior designers face similar AI exposure, but AI is more complementary to interior designers than to customer service representatives, because interior designers’ work involves more unstructured tasks and requires more frequent physical presence at worksites that currently cannot be fully automated by AI. Following Pizzinelli et al. (2023), we construct two scores by combining each occupation’s AI exposure index with its complementarity profile. We believe the FOMC may now regret having eased policy in 2025. These rate cuts were predicated on a view that the labor market was abruptly weakening – "flashing red" – based on a low payroll growth rate and so required policy stimulus. Recent Fed research (including papers on 31 March from the Dallas Fed and 2 April from the Board staff) suggests a volte-face in this assessment: they now seem to think the labor market was instead performing stably through that period, in line with labor supply. The natural next step to this reversal in view is likely greater openness to the idea that last year’s rate cuts may have left the policy stance too easy. The unemployment rate was near rounding to 4.2% in March. If it declines further, especially in the context of the current persistent inflation problem, envisioning rate hikes becomes easier. This surge drove substantial job creation and strong activity across various services industries. However, growth in services has since moderated as the "catch-up" effect in hiring faded and the period of "revenge spending" by consumers ran its course. Recent readings point to more moderate growth in service providing sectors. The business activity index fell 6 points to 53.9. It has remained in expansion for most months post-COVID, though the pace has gradually slowed over the past five years. Services activity had rebounded since November last year, but the March data broke that trend. Current readings remain somewhat below the 2010–2019 average of 58.7. The employment index fell sharply to 45.2, down 6.6 points from February, following three consecutive months of improvement. Our base case is that GenAI will be a net labor augmenting technology — one that is disruptive but ultimately raises productivity and real wages. There are certainly risks of a broader disruption to labor markets aligning to outsized job losses. Our analysis seeks to verify the likeliest path of AI impacting the labor market by finding micro-signals in macroeconomic data; we do this through our dashboard. Because no single indicator can fully capture labor market dynamics, the tracker is structured as a dashboard of key indicators (see Exhibit 2 ). The dashboard evaluates how AI is affecting the labor market in real time through a series of market trackers derived from a combination of traditional statistical inferences from employment surveys from both households and firms as well as alternative AI exposure measures with big data as derived by our Morgan Stanley Thematic team. Our aim is to publish regular updates to shed light on underlying trends as they emerge. Measurement is complicated because GenAI’s impact on labor demand is double- edged: The same technology that can automate tasks can also augment labor, raise productivity, and increase demand in exposed areas of the economy. records.text: M Foundation 36 The internet was incubated in the 1960s military-academic network (ARPANET) before morphing into a commercial and mass-market network by the 1990s with the advent of the World Wide Web. By 2000, about half of US households had internet access. Other digital technologies like mobile phones and enterprise software systems further shaped this wave. In short, by the turn of the 21st century the US had entered the Information Age, where creation, processing, and transmission of information became central economic activities. The transition from an agrarian to industrial to knowledge-based economy was largely complete. Investment shifts to Intangible Capital During the fifth innovation wave, digital technologies further shifted the composition of business investment toward intangible assets like software, databases, algorithms, brand capital, and intellectual property. These items now represent a substantial and growing share of business investment (Corrado, Hulten, and Sichel 2005). Looking further out, we see a silver lining. Before tensions began, Asia was operating from a position of cyclical strength. The spread of factories dramatically increased the scale and efficiency of producing goods, moving production out of homes and small workshops into centralized mills. Cotton textiles became America’s first major factory industry, especially in New England, benefiting from southern cotton supplies and protective tariffs against British imports. The federal government played a role in nurturing early industry by contracting with manufacturers, which supplemented private demand and kick-started production at private firms. Equally transformative were improvements in transportation infrastructure. The early 19th century saw massive investment in turnpikes, canals, and steamboats, followed by railroads from the 1830s onward. These projects required significant capital (much of it raised by state governments or private investors) and often led to speculative booms and busts.

LLC US Daily: Breaking Down the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Substitution vs. Augmentation 4 April 2026 | 10:02PM EDT We have used a measure of how exposed an occupation’s work activities are to n artificial intelligence to track AI’s impact on the labor market. Recent research adds a second dimension by estimating how complementary AI is to human labor in performing each work activity in order to distinguish activities where AI is likely to substitute for human labor from activities where it is likely to augment it. These measures are similar to our AI displacement scores but a bit more detailed. We combine AI exposure scores with an AI complementarity index developed by IMF economists to dig deeper into AI’s impact on the labor market so far. We find that since the launch of ChatGPT, industries and occupations facing high n AI substitution risk have experienced a decline in payroll employment and a larger increase in unemployment rates than less AI-exposed industries, with younger and less experienced workers hit hardest. At the same time, industries and occupations more exposed to AI augmentation have seen an increase in payroll employment and a modest decline in unemployment rates, partially offsetting the negative substitution effects. records.text: US Economics Weekly3 April 2026 ab 10 Economic Comment: labor market disruption II As a follow up to our recent notes on AI disruption and the labor market, we consider the "hollowing out" narrative, which has been revisited alongside the prospect of AI's potential productivity driven disruption. The thought of labor obsolescence in the wake of labor-replacing AI technology has rekindled concerns for the displacement of a range of service sector workers. Most often, the phrase refers to loss of demand for certain types of labor, and opportunities lost in the Midwest and Rust Belt as manufacturing jobs left. That observation also underpins some of the current policy motivation for re- industrialization. Also, the loss of domestic manufacturing, leaving behind shells of smaller cities, has not just affected parts of the United States but has shared elements elsewhere in developed market countries, like France for example. Globalization gets a lot of blame. However, in this note we show that labor-replacing technological advancement and efficiencies likely played at least as large a role. That may offer some insight as we look ahead to the potential for AI-related displacement of workers. records.text: As concerns about the labor market impact of AI grow, we draw on four decades n of individual-level data to assess the short- and long-term “scarring” effects of being displaced by technology. We identify occupations disrupted by technology in each decade since 1980 and use the National Longitudinal Surveys—which follow over 20,000 individuals born in the 1950–60s and 1980s over their entire lives—to track the labor market outcomes of workers employed in these disrupted occupations. We draw four main conclusions. First, workers displaced from n technology-disrupted occupations face more difficult short-run transitions back into employment. They take approximately one month longer to find a new job and suffer real earnings losses of more than 3% upon reemployment, compared with negligible losses for workers displaced from more stable occupations. A key mechanism behind these worse outcomes is occupational downgrading. Workers displaced by technology are more likely to move into more routine occupations requiring fewer analytical and interpersonal skills, likely because the same technological shifts that eliminated their positions also eroded the value of their existing skills. Second, the effects of technological displacement are long-lasting. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 Executive summary Five Innovation Waves Before AI: Common Patterns and Lessons The current AI wave has led to both optimism and pessimism: it promises faster productivity and economic growth, but also raises concerns about job displacement, inequality, and social upheaval. In assessing what AI may mean for the US economy, we look to the past for guidance. After all, as the saying goes, history may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Over the past 250 years, the US has experienced five major innovation waves: • The First Industrial Revolution (factories, steam, canals, railroads) • Steam, Railroads, and Steel • Electrification and the Internal Combustion Engine • Electronics and Aviation • The Internet and Digital Networks Across these waves, a consistent pattern emerges between innovation and macroeconomic transformation: transformative technologies initially disrupt labor markets and financial systems, provoke political responses, and widen inequality – but they ultimately raise productivity, expand output, and fundamentally reshape the structure of the economy. A look at prior innovation waves suggests that while technological revolutions invariably bring short-term disruptions and uncertainty, they also deliver significant long-run benefits. However, how those benefits are distributed – narrowly or broadly – depends on how policymakers, businesses, and educators manage the transition. Common Themes Across the Five Innovation Waves

records.text: M Foundation 16 The Second Wave: Steam, Railroads, and Steel (1830-1910) Technological Breakthroughs and Timeline The second innovation wave in US history unfolded from the 1830s through the early 20th century. Often termed the “Second Industrial Revolution,” this innovation wave was driven by steam power, railroads, steel production, and heavy machinery. The late 19th century also witnessed major advances in communications. Many enabling technologies of the modern industrial economy either emerged or reached maturity in this period, including: • The railroad network expanded spectacularly after the US Civil War. Track mileage grew from about 30,000 miles in 1860 to roughly 192,000 miles by 1900, connecting regions into an integrated national market (Fogel 1964). The completion of the first transcontinental railroad in 1869 sharply reduced coast- to-coast travel times and accelerated western settlement. • Steam power became widespread in both transportation and manufacturing, freeing factories from dependence on water power and enabling urban industrial growth (Chandler 1977). • The development of mass-produced steel revolutionized construction and manufacturing. Steel rails lowered railroad costs, while steel was increasingly used in bridges, machinery, ships, and skyscrapers. • The commercial telegraph, the telephone, and early electrification reduced coordination costs and transformed business organization.
