records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 7 Tracking the AI Effect in Labor Markets The impact of generative AI (GenAI) on labor demand appears to be binary — see Acemoglu (2021) for a framework. On the one hand, occupations that are fully automatable may eventually be performed almost entirely by GenAI. Taken to the extreme, productivity could turn explosive as AI automates both production and innovation, leading to large-scale displacement of labor (Korninek 2024). However, displacement is far less clear-cut when only some tasks within an occupation can be performed by AI. In such cases, AI can augment labor, boosting productivity and potentially increasing demand for those occupations rather than eliminating them. Some fears of displacement by AI have failed to materialize: In radiology, for example, augmentation effects have dominated. Roughly a decade ago, Geoffrey Hinton (a computer scientist, often referred to as the "Godfather of AI") predicted that AI would soon be able to perform essentially all tasks done by radiologists. His prediction proved inaccurate: the number of radiologists has increased, and wages have risen over the past ten years. On the other hand, the tractor stands as a clear historical example of technology displacement. It was introduced in 1900 but broadly adopted after the First World War, from 1920 to 1970. If GenAI ultimately transforms labor markets, we would expect signs of either task augmentation or displacement, alongside evidence of AI adoption and changing occupational tasks. The open question is how quickly firms are modifying production processes. CPS data show that reported task changes rose sharply after COVID, largely reflecting elevated job switching. records.text: 3 April 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 12 Deutsche Bank AG Additionally, the Collateral-in-Lieu (CIL) service, approved in December 2025 by the SEC, has potential to generate more capacity to alleviate borrowing constraints. This service enables the CCP (FICC) to take a lien on the repo collateral instead of requiring a separate margin, thereby reducing overall margin costs. Furthermore, this lien would obviate the need for FICC to require dealers to guarantee the performance of the cash lender they are sponsoring, leading to a reduction in capital costs and freeing up RWA-constrained dealers to intermediate more repo. As more dealers onboard to this new platform over the next year and trading volumes in sponsored GC grow, we anticipate gradual abatement of month- and quarter-end pressures. Should the aforementioned month-end intermediation challenges be resolved fully (SOFR-RRP spreads staying at the average levels between days 7 and 17), we estimate a decline of approximately 1bp in monthly SOFR fixing averages, all else equal. records.text: The second reason why we think the concerns for political risk are likely overstated has to do with the support that the government, and the PM’s party in particular, still enjoys in opinion polls. Over the last three months opinion polls have pointed to some erosion in political support, but the ruling coalition and the Prime Minister’s party still poll above the share of votes they received in the 2022 election. This is a distinctive feature of the current government (Exhibit 9, left). It seems that the ruling coalition is in no rush to call an early election and, if anything, we think the opposite is the case. A recent defection of some far-right MPs from the ruling coalition established a new fringe party (Futuro Nazionale) in open competition with two of the parties (Fratelli d’Italia and Lega) in the coalition government. According to opinion polls, the new party is currently polling around 3.5%, and mostly absorbing votes from the parties in the parliamentary majority. The ruling coalition needs time to attempt to reverse this trend and, if it were able to recover even a share of the lost votes, it would likely achieve enough support to win even against a broader coalition among opposition parties (Exhibit 9, right). Therefore, we see no immediate challenge to government stability. If the productivity gains materialize, and AI proves labor replacing, logically it would follow that job destruction rates will almost surely rise in that case. However, can the higher rates of overall growth, and higher rates of overall income, feed back into a range of sectors and drive job creation? Historically that has been the case in the US. But that will also pose important policy questions and challenges. In this note we have abstracted from labor's share of national income, and the real wage gains of production and non-supervisory workers, and other issues of relative bargaining strength. We will address that in a future essay, but productivity growth should raise real wages for some workers, but issues of relative inequality and the feedback loops elsewhere will also be important questions to consider. However, that AI disruption necessarily implies meaningfully higher and more persistent unemployment is not the case. That will also depend upon other policies, how they address job creation or regulation, address dynamism, and overall economic growth and other feedback loops through the economy. What the rapid productivity growth in manufacturing taught us is that economic change comes with disruption and risk of displacement, but that does not mean overall employment and growth outcomes need to suffer. records.text: 2. Technological Displacement Has Long-Lasting Negative Effects The labor market effects of technological displacement are persistent. We estimate these effects over the ten years following a job loss by matching technology-displaced workers with comparable workers who lost their jobs in non-disrupted occupations and with never-displaced workers3 via a propensity score matching approach—with workers paired according to their pre-displacement characteristics4—and computing the average gap in outcomes across matched pairs. As the left panel of Exhibit 6 shows, real earnings for technology-displaced workers decline more sharply on impact and never fully recover, lagging those of never-displaced workers by slightly under 10pp a decade after displacement and those of other displaced workers by roughly 5pp. The probability of experiencing a subsequent unemployment spell also remains persistently higher, particularly in the first five years (Exhibit 6, right panel). The scarring effects extend beyond labor market outcomes. Focusing on workers displaced early in their careers—between the ages of 25 and 35—we find that technological displacement meaningfully slows wealth accumulation relative to other workers (Exhibit 7, left panel). This effect is largely driven by delayed homeownership, as lower earnings and persistent job instability constrain displaced workers’ ability to save and invest. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 33 supported, in part, by strong unions, progressive taxation, high marginal tax rates, and the broad diffusion of secondary and higher education (Goldin and Margo 1992). The institutional framework built during the third innovation wave—collective bargaining under the Wagner Act, Social Security, and mass public education—ensured that productivity gains from electrification and mass production translated into rising middle- class wages. However, by the late 1970s this equilibrium began to shift. Wage inequality began to widen sharply in the 1980s, marking what many economic historians view as a tipping point in the postwar distributional regime. Skill-biased technological change associated with computing and early automation increased the premium to college education, while globalization and import competition placed downward pressure on routine manufacturing wages (Autor, Katz, and Krueger 1998; Autor, Dorn, and Hanson 2013). At the same time, declining union density, deregulation, and reduced progressivity in taxation weakened the mechanisms that had previously compressed wage dispersion. The result was a sustained rise in top income shares and capital income concentration after 1980, reversing much of the mid-century equalization (Piketty and Saez 2003). Mid-century manufacturing shows measurable gains in labor productivity and total factor productivity linked to mechanization and the “American System” of standardized, interchangeable parts, which reduced reliance on skilled artisans and enabled larger-scale output (Hounshell 1984; Atack and Bateman 1999). Higher productivity eventually translated into rising output, real wages, and living standards, though early gains were uneven. In both Britain and the United States, real wages rose only slowly relative to output per worker during the initial decades of the industrial revolution. In Britain this became known as the “Engels’ Pause,” implying a temporary decline in labor’s share based on observations made by Friedrich Engels in 1845 (Allen 2009; Lindert and Williamson 1983). However, by the mid-19th century at the end of the first industrial revolution, US real wages were clearly trending upward, and manufactured goods such as textiles and tools became cheaper and more widely accessible (Lindert and Williamson 1983; Carter et al. 2006). records.text: the US labor market, though the process was gradual and regionally uneven. In 1800, the vast majority of Americans lived on farms or relied on craft production. By 1860, over half of the labor force still worked in agriculture, but the farm share had declined to roughly 53 percent as industrial and service employment expanded in cities (Atack, Bateman, and Weiss 1980; Carter et al. 2006). Lebergott (1966) reports similar figures. In 1800 he shows that 74% of Americans worked in agriculture. 1 By 1850, the share of farm employment slipped to 55%, while nonfarm employment stood at 45%. By the mid-1850s, the absolute number of workers engaged primarily in agriculture had begun to level off, while employment in manufacturing and construction more than doubled between 1820 and 1860 (Atack and Bateman 1999). One distinct alteration in the labor market was the shift from a skilled workforce to low- skilled or semi-skilled workforce. The new factories hired unskilled or semi-skilled workers, including women and children, to operate machines, sometimes displacing traditional artisans and home-based craftsmen. For example, water-powered textile mills in New England used relatively unskilled labor, including young farm women recruited under the Lowell system, to produce cloth at scale, reducing demand for skilled 1. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

Transformative technologies initially disrupt labor markets and financial systems, provoke political responses, and widen inequality. But they ultimately raise productivity, expand output, and fundamentally reshape the economy. records.text: 3 April 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 46 Deutsche Bank AG Quarter-end pension rebalancing estimates We expect relatively subdued pension demand for fixed income securities at quarter-end, reflecting the significant declines in equities and the relative outperformance of bonds this quarter. Through March 30, the S&P 500 has fallen by 6.7%, compared to a more modest 0.8% decline in the Bloomberg US Aggregate Index. This marks only the fourth instance in the past 25 quarters in which equities underperformed bonds. Under a static-weight framework, this likely resulted in a ~1.2-1.5% shift in portfolio weights, implying a mechanical bias toward equity buying and fixed income selling into quarter-end. A simple estimate using Q4 pension asset levels implies potential fixed income selling of around $47bn, including ~$30bn from public pensions and ~$17bn from private pensions. However, incorporating historical rebalancing flows and asset growth reduces the implied selling materially, with our forecast model pointing to potentially $3bn of net buying in fixed income securities. For historical reference, in Q1 2025 when equities underperformed bonds by a similarly large margin (-7.1%), pension flows into fixed income remained positive at ~$13bn, although modest relative to prior quarters. US Economics March employment: A strong report The latest estimates show a strong payroll gain of 178k, even though the headline print was exaggerated by the end of a strike and birth/death adjustments. The unemployment rate fell notably, mainly reflecting slowing labor supply. Estimates point to a moderation in income growth. • March's employment estimates were strong, essentially reversing February's weak print. The BLS reported a 178k gain in nonfarm payroll employment (Barclays: 50k; consensus: 65k), reversing all of February's 133k decline, and the unemployment rate fell 0.1pp, to a thin 4.3%. The private sector jobs estimate swung similarly, with March's 186k gain flipping from February's 129k decline. To be sure, the upswing in March's estimate is exaggerated somewhat by the return of striking workers at Kaiser Permanente in California that temporarily sidelined 31k healthcare workers in February. Nonetheless, the data are consistent with a moderate underlying trajectory of nonfarm payroll employment: the 3mma gain was 68k/m in March, well above the 39k/m decline during the preceding three-month period ended in December, though that had been affected by the October government shutdown and "fork-in the-road" option for government employees. • As in January, birth-death adjustments to the payroll estimates appear to have contributed to the surprising strength in the March employment estimate

records.text: M Foundation 32 dubbed the “productivity slowdown.” Gordon (2016) argues that several forces contributed to the slowdown. First, the oil shocks of 1973–74 and 1979 sharply raised energy prices (a large relative price shock to a critical input), reducing measured productivity by forcing costly adjustments in energy-intensive industries and reallocating capital toward less productive uses. Second, Gordon saw the extraordinary one-time gains from electrification, motorization, and urban infrastructure as largely exhausted by the early 1970s. Some scholars argue that intangible investments and free digital services are imperfectly reflected in GDP statistics, potentially understating true gains (the "productivity paradox"). Other economists emphasize diffusion lags and argue frontier firms experienced strong productivity growth, while lagging firms struggled to fully integrate digital tools. As in prior innovation waves, aggregate productivity performance reflects both technological potential and the speed with which complementary skills, management practices, and regulatory frameworks adjust. Productivity accelerated, offsetting a demographic-drive slowdown in hours worked As we introduced in our prior research (see Immigration and the Macroeconomy), we estimate potential growth using a trend-cycle decomposition framework. The framework assumes each measure of economic activity and labor markets is represented as the sum of cyclical and trend components, where the cyclical component is assumed to be common across all the inputs with contemporaneous effects. Each variable is permitted to have its own unique trend. The framework yields estimates of potential output, the building blocks of potential output, the output gap, long-run unemployment, and the equilibrium real policy rate, which are key inputs to monetary and fiscal policy. records.text: M Foundation 8 The First Wave: The Industrial Revolution (late 18th to mid- 19th century) Technological progress has been a driving force behind US economic growth and transformation since the nation’s founding. History reveals a sequence of major innovation waves, each centered on a cluster of breakthrough technologies, that fundamentally altered the structure of the U.S. economy and society. From the first Industrial Revolution in the early 1800s to the late-20th-century digital revolution, these waves of innovation have spurred rapid increases in productivity and output, redefined how and where people work, and raised living standards over time. The innovation waves also brought periods of disruption: old industries declined as new ones emerged, workers’ skills fell into or out of demand, and communities and policymakers struggled to adjust. This report examines five pivotal innovation waves in U.S. economic history, with a focus on their transformative technologies, effects on business investment and infrastructure, impacts on the labor market and skills, boom-bust dynamics, changes in productivity, and broader social and political responses (including evolving patterns of inequality, public sentiment toward technological change, and shifts in education). Understanding these historical episodes provides a valuable perspective on what looks to be the sixth major innovation wave in the US – artificial intelligence – and how its benefits and challenges might be navigated. Public concern about misinformation, platform governance, and the influence of large technology firms on democratic processes have intensified. These have become features of the US public debate and the debate in other western democracies. Governments, generally speaking, have responded with regulatory initiatives targeting digital competition and cross-border data flows. As in earlier innovation waves, rapid structural change has generated both optimism about productivity gains and concern about inequality, job security, and social cohesion. In the 1990s and early 2000s, many observers argued that the internet would decentralize information, lower entry barriers to speech, and strengthen democratic participation by empowering individuals relative to gatekeepers (Benkler 2006; Shirky 2008). More recently, however, research has highlighted countervailing forces like algorithmic bias, network effects, and platform concentration that have often amplified misinformation and political polarization (Allcott and Gentzkow 2017; Sunstein 2018). At the same time, academic studies point to rising social isolation and declines in civic engagement that may be associated with digital substitution for face-to-face interaction (Putnam 2000; Twenge 2017). Prior overinvestment cycles were related to unprofitable investments infrastructure and other physical capital and the dot-com bubble mimicked these characteristics in intangible capital. The era saw speculative enthusiasm surrounding transformative technologies. Equity valuations of internet firms rose rapidly before collapsing. However, the underlying infrastructure comprised of fiber networks, data centers, and software systems, provided the foundation for subsequent recovery. Venture capital funding surged again in the 2010s around social media, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence, reflecting recurring cycles of exuberance and consolidation. Low interest rates and abundant liquidity likely amplified valuations, while expectations of network dominance drove capital toward a small set of firms. A key conclusion from our perspective is that financial markets both accelerate diffusion by funding risky ventures and amplify volatility when expectations adjust. The consequences are clear: between 1900 and 1970 the share of US employment in agriculture fell from about 40% to under 5%.1 Calibrating AI Exposure To analyze potential labor market disruptions, we classify occupations by their exposure to AI using the framework developed by Felten et al. (2021). Felten and co- authors construct an AI exposure index by assessing how tasks within each occupation align with current and anticipated AI capabilities. This measure is forward-looking, as it attempts to forecast future effects based on progress in various AI applications. In other words, what we see in labor markets today can change over time. The AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index uses AI abilities across ten domains, ranging from image and speech recognition to real-time game playing. These ability scores are combined into an index measuring how well AI might perform the tasks associated with each occupation. The index is standardized as a z-score. We group occupations into three categories based on their AIOE values: Low exposure groups form the bottom 25% of the distribution, medium exposure the middle 50%, and high exposure the top 25%. Importantly, this indicator measures exposure, not realized disruption. Early phases of innovation often widen disparities as capital deepening and new skill premiums benefit early adopters. The Gilded Age exemplified extreme concentration. The mid-20th century stands out as an exception: electrification and mass production coincided with the “Great Compression,” supported by unions, progressive taxation, and expanding education. The digital revolution reversed that compression. Since 1980, income and wealth concentration have risen sharply, driven by returns to capital, skill-biased technical change, and public policy choices that reversed Great Compression-era policy. Innovation itself does not predetermine inequality: institutions and public policy mediate how gains are distributed. Education has been a decisive adaptation mechanism. Each previous wave raised the return to human capital, and each time the United States expanded education in response. The common school movement followed early industrialization. Land-grant universities professionalized engineering and agricultural science. The high school movement and GI Bill democratized secondary and higher education. The digital age intensified demand for STEM skills and lifelong learning. When education expanded broadly, productivity gains translated into shared prosperity. records.text: know – we point to several lessons from prior innovation waves: 1. Productivity Gains Are Likely: AI, like prior general-purpose technologies, should raise output per worker, particularly if combined with organizational redesign. 2. Labor Displacement Is Transitional, Not Permanent: Past fears of mass technological unemployment did not materialize. Job composition changes, some jobs die away, others emerge, but employment persists. 3. Boom-Bust Cycles Are Probable: Heavy AI infrastructure investment (compute, data centers, power centers) resembles prior railroad and telecom buildouts. Financial excess and volatility are likely. 4. Inequality Risks Are Elevated: AI’s scalability and data network effects may intensify concentration. Without policy intervention, returns to capital and top talent could widen gaps. Income and wealth inequality are already as high as they have been in the last 125 years. We think the risk of social and political divisions remain elevated. 5. Education and Re-skilling Will Be Decisive: Every successful transition required expanding education, but also altering how education is provided. After the labor market, the sector that may end up adjusting the most is education. AI may require lifelong learning systems, not just traditional degree pathways. 6. Policy Matters: Antitrust, social insurance, and human capital investment shaped outcomes in prior waves. Institutional adaptation determines whether gains are broadly shared.

The erosion of the post-war, US-led international order, based on multilateral cooperation and treaties, has brought a shift back toward nation-states pursuing their own interests. Unlike past conflicts, it has been difficult to forge a coordinated alliance to take collective action against Iran as diplomatic negotiations have yet to gain real traction. Workers in these occupations tend to be more educated, earn higher average household incomes, and perform tasks that are largely computer based. Much of the work involves information processing, quantitative analysis, document review, or standardized decision making. Examples include financial analysts, actuaries, accountants, and judicial clerks. • Low exposure occupations (18%) are predominantly blue collar and involve hands on, physical work carried out in non standardized environments. The least exposed jobs in this group rely heavily on physical presence, dexterity, and real time human interaction — such as dancers, performers, and many construction workers. Relatively more exposed occupations within this low exposure group are those that combine manual work with a specific technical or diagnostic knowledge component, such as equipment installers and repairers. • Medium exposure occupations (56%) sit between these two extremes and tend to be a heterogeneous mix of jobs that combine manual and cognitive tasks. These occupations often involve some routine, computer mediated work alongside non routine physical or interpersonal activities, making them partially susceptible to automation while remaining difficult to fully replace. records.text: We then study the labor market outcomes of workers in these technology-disrupted occupations using individual-level data from the National Longitudinal Surveys. These nationally representative surveys, sponsored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), follow over 20,000 US individuals comprising two cohorts—the first born in the 1950-1960s and followed from 1979 to 2022, and the second born in the 1980s and followed from 1997 to 2021.2 This dataset allows us to track workers’ full occupational histories. As an illustration, Exhibit 3 shows the occupations into which workers employed as statistical clerks or machine operators in the 1980s—two roles heavily disrupted by technology— transitioned over subsequent decades. So the causal variables to employment and productivity may be mixed currently. We view the digital revolution associated with the internet as a useful benchmark for anchoring expectations. As discussed in our note on Technological Waves, AI is only the latest in a series of technologically driven disruptions in US labor markets. Historical instances saw disruption play out over decades, though the introduction of the internet saw a quicker adoption from technology to labor force, driving productivity gains in relatively short period. We expect the AI phase to be even faster. The headline takeaway from our work is that aggregate disruption still looks modest, which might be reflecting the early stage of AI adoption.
